title: Select how long to keep the MySQL standby for a rollback
summary: After the switch, reverse replication keeps MySQL in sync, so the shop can go back. The plan recommends a 7-day rollback window, which covers one full weekly cycle.

blocks.title: The problem
blocks.html: After the switch, new orders go to PostgreSQL only. A rollback needs a MySQL copy that is up to date. Reverse replication keeps this copy up to date, but only while it runs.

blocks.title: What we found
blocks.html:
• [READ] The settlement job runs each Friday night. The invoice run is on the 1st of each month. [src: report.md]
  • [INFERRED] The MySQL instances cost about $137 per day while they run. [src: report.md]
  • [UNVERIFIED] A rollback takes about 20 minutes. Nobody has rehearsed it yet (F6).

blocks.title: What the window costs
blocks.html:
While the window is open:

  • The schema freeze continues (D4).
  • The service cannot use PostgreSQL-only features, because the release must also run on MySQL (F1).
  • The MySQL instances keep costing money.

figures.caption: The rollback path. Reverse replication keeps the MySQL standby in sync until the window ends. A rollback switches the connection back in about 20 minutes (not rehearsed yet).

options.label: 48 hours
options.detail_html: Cost: about $274. Covers: the first weekend only. The Friday settlement job runs after the window ends.

options.label: 7 days
options.detail_html: Cost: about $960. Covers: one full weekly cycle, with the Friday settlement job and one weekend.

options.label: 30 days
options.detail_html: Cost: about $7,000: $4,100 for the instances, plus one more month of the MySQL 5.7 support fee. Covers: the invoice run on 1 February. The schema freeze lasts 35 days in total.

recommendation_html: Option b. Most problems after a database move show in the first full weekly cycle. For the monthly invoice run, a test in staging before the cutover costs less than a 30-day window.

facts.label: Depends on
facts.value: D1 (option b gives the reverse path)
